entries.test: Whether, as of May 2025, any international AI governance body was operating with binding implementation, whether the US had a dedicated national AI agency, and whether federal AI-cybercrime capacity (e.g., CISA staffing and programs) had been cut.
entries.note: The cybercrime part is vaguer than the other two, but reports on CISA cuts and agency changes give it a plain reading.

entries.test: FBI IC3, FTC and industry reports on how much AI-enabled fraud grew from 2023 to 2025, and whether any coordinated federal policy or legislation on AI scams existed by May 2025.
entries.note: The 'by many accounts' hedge only covers the growth in scams; the claim that there is no federal response is stated flatly.

entries.test: Republican positions and votes on AI regulation in 2023 versus 2025, including support for the proposed 10-year moratorium on state AI laws and the administration's AI deregulation orders.
entries.note: 'Drowned out' is loose wording, but the comparison between 2023 and 2025 can be tested against the public record.

entries.test: The transcript of Altman's May 8, 2025 Senate Commerce Committee testimony compared with his May 16, 2023 testimony on whether he supports AI regulation.
entries.note: 'At every turn' is an exaggeration; the core claim is that his position reversed, which can be checked.
This is a judgment of Altman's character, and it rests on whether he privately means what he says, which public evidence cannot show.
The proposition fills in the answer ('he cannot be trusted'), which the context implies but Marcus never states. Whether someone can be trusted is a value judgment.
